clue.text: Artist acquires constituency

parts.note: to acquire something is to gain it, so acquires gives gains
a borough is a town that once returned its own Member of Parliament, a parliamentary constituency

explanation.surface: A painter wins himself a parliamentary seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gainsborough was the eighteenth-century English portrait and landscape painter.

clue.text: Kings of Victorian literature

parts.note: four Hanoverian kings shared one name, and so did several leading Victorian novelists: Eliot, Meredith, Gissing, du Maurier

explanation.surface: The great names who ruled nineteenth-century letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kings' reads as 'leading figures', but it points to the royal Georges I to IV; the Victorian writers George Eliot, George Meredith and George Gissing give the literary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural first name was borne both by four British monarchs and by many Victorian authors.

clue.text: Not what the Impressionists did, surely?

definitions.text: Not what the Impressionists did, surely?

parts.words: Not what the Impressionists did, surely?
parts.note: Monet and friends rendered their own impressions of light rather than copying; a stage impressionist, by contrast, mimics people for a living

explanation.surface: A sly question about whether the French painters merely copied nature.
explanation.walkthrough: The painters are the surface sense; the stage impressionist, who mimics voices, is what the answer describes, so the question mark flags the double reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To copy or mimic someone is the stage impressionist's trade, which the painters claimed not to do.

clue.text: Combination of ideas in dissertation on Thorndyke's smuggling vicar?

indicators.note: in this down clue one piece is placed on top of the other, so the vicar's name heads the word

parts.note: Dr Syn, the smuggling parson of Dymchurch, is the hero of Russell Thorndike's novels
a thesis is a dissertation written for a degree

explanation.surface: A doctoral thesis about the fictional smuggling clergyman, combining several ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Syn is the vicar of Dymchurch who secretly leads a smuggling gang in Russell Thorndike's novels (the clue spells the author Thorndyke).
explanation.definitionFit: In philosophy, a synthesis unites separate ideas or a thesis and antithesis into one whole.

clue.text: Mary McCarthy's refreshment centre on the sands?

definitions.meaning: the American writer Mary McCarthy published the satirical novella The ... in 1949
a fertile watered spot in a desert where travellers drink and rest

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one word: McCarthy's book title, and the watered resting place in a desert.

clue.text: By the help of canvas wings … proposes to fly — - -from Dover to Calais " (The Fool of Quality, Henry Brooke)

definitions.text: By the help of canvas wings … proposes to fly — - -from Dover to Calais " (The Fool of Quality, Henry Brooke)

parts.words: By the help of canvas wings … proposes to fly — - -from Dover to Calais " (The Fool of Quality, Henry Brooke)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing word means across the water, as a sailing crossing of the Channel would be

explanation.walkthrough: A literary fill-in: the solver supplies the hyphenated word from Henry Brooke's novel The Fool of Quality; flying between Dover and Calais is a crossing of the English Channel.
explanation.definitionFit: Going from Dover to Calais means crossing the Channel, so the voyage is across the water, abroad.

clue.text: Puppet embodying the spirit of 20, may be grand in melodrama

definitions.meaning: the Lyon glove-puppet character, a mischievous figure of disorder, fits the spirit of the clue at 20
the Grand ... was the Paris theatre famous for gory melodrama

explanation.walkthrough: '20' refers to the answer at 20-down, the spirit of disorder that the puppet embodies.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the anarchic French puppet hero and to half of the name of the Parisian horror theatre.

clue.text: Permit trivia, perhaps, in Rousseau's work

indicators.note: perhaps says the preceding two words are one possible arrangement, so their letters may be reordered

explanation.surface: Allowing trifles is what the French philosopher's writing does, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges PERMIT TRIVIA. The Rousseau is not the philosopher Jean-Jacques but the painter Henri Rousseau, 'Le Douanier', the best-known naive painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Rousseau painted in a naive, untrained style, the category known by this name.

clue.text: Like an island statue

parts.note: the Colossus, a wonder of the ancient world, stood at the harbour of an Aegean island; this adjective means of that island

explanation.surface: Something resembling a statue standing on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means belonging to the island of the Colossus, the famous ancient statue.

clue.text: Notice porcelain it may not be genuine

parts.note: to notice something is to see it
Ming is the fine porcelain of the Ming dynasty of China

explanation.surface: Spot a valuable vase, though it may be a fake.
explanation.definitionFit: An outward appearance, as in 'the seeming of things', is a show that may not be real.

clue.text: Matriarch and patriarch who produced 7

parts.note: a grandma is a matriarch, the elder woman of a family
Moses is one of the Old Testament patriarchs

explanation.surface: A grandmother figure and a Biblical leader responsible for the answer at 7.
explanation.walkthrough: '7' is the answer at 7-down; Anna Mary Robertson Moses, the American folk painter, began painting in her seventies.
explanation.definitionFit: The American folk artist was the most celebrated naive painter of her country.

clue.text: War dramatist gets medal at German stronghold

parts.note: MC is the Military Cross, a British gallantry medal
a rath is an ancient Irish earthwork fort, a stronghold

explanation.surface: A playwright of war is decorated at an enemy fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: John McGrath wrote 'Events While Guarding the Bofors Gun'; 'at' is a link joining the medal to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: John McGrath, the Scottish playwright, wrote dramas about soldiering and war.

clue.text: Ms Sontag not applicable as apocryphal wife

parts.note: Susan Sontag was the American essayist and critic
NA is the abbreviation for not applicable on forms

explanation.surface: The American critic is irrelevant as a wife in a doubtful story.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Apocrypha's story of the elders, the virtuous married woman falsely accused is Joakim's spouse.

clue.text: Shelagh Delaney's was of Pooh Bear's choice

definitions.text: Shelagh Delaney's was of Pooh Bear's choice

parts.words: Shelagh Delaney's was of Pooh Bear's choice
parts.note: Delaney's play title is 'A ... of Honey', and honey is what Winnie-the-Pooh always prefers

explanation.surface: The playwright's sample came from the bear's favourite food.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelagh Delaney's 1958 play is 'A Taste of Honey'; Pooh Bear's choice is honey, so the clue reads the title with honey supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sample or flavour of something, which in Delaney's title is of honey.

clue.text: Shod like Felix Randal's horses?

parts.note: Hopkins's farrier Felix Randal fettled for the great grey drayhorse 'his bright and battering sandal', so the poem calls a horseshoe a sandal

explanation.surface: How the blacksmith's horses in the poem were shod.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gerard Manley Hopkins's poem 'Felix Randal', the farrier makes the drayhorse 'his bright and battering sandal', a horseshoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing open shoes held by straps, which Hopkins's poem applies to the horseshoe.

clue.text: He ended his days in deep reflection

definitions.text: He ended his days in deep reflection

parts.words: He ended his days in deep reflection
parts.note: the Greek youth of myth fell in love with his own image in a pool and pined away gazing at it; deep reflection reads as thought but means a mirrored image in water

explanation.surface: A man who spent his last years in profound thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deep reflection' looks like contemplation, but it is the image in a deep pool, where the youth of Greek myth died staring at himself.
explanation.definitionFit: In Ovid, the self-loving youth wasted away beside a pool, gazing at his own image.

clue.text: It gets steamed up over Paris' manoeuvres

indicators.note: manoeuvres says the preceding letters are moved about into a new order

parts.note: the possessive adds no letter, so this is just the city name

explanation.surface: Something gets heated about events in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manoeuvres' rearranges OVER and PARIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that turns liquid into vapour, so it is filled with steam.

clue.text: Posthumous servant, "a sly and constant knave"

definitions.meaning: in Shakespeare's Cymbeline the hero Posthumus Leonatus has a loyal servant
the Queen in Cymbeline calls this servant 'a sly and constant knave', constant to his master

explanation.walkthrough: The clue spells 'Posthumous', but the master in Cymbeline is Posthumus Leonatus.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe the same Cymbeline character: the servant of Posthumus, whom the Queen insults.

clue.text: Précis for the poorly

definitions.meaning: a summary of the main points, a quick review
tired and unwell, as in feeling worn out

explanation.definitionFit: One word means both a brief summary and the state of being worn out and unwell.

clue.text: A doctor in Georgia comes to a stop

indicators.note: in says the first pieces are placed inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A physician in the American South is halted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes to' links wordplay to definition; the stop is an organ stop, not a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ register imitating the viol, named after the viola da gamba.

clue.text: Somehow go zonal to find Neapolitan counsellor

indicators.note: somehow says the next words are rearranged by some unstated means

explanation.surface: Travel through regions to find an adviser from Naples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges ZONAL into NZALO, placed after GO.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Tempest, the honest old counsellor of the King of Naples bears this name.

clue.text: Lemur is set free in disorder happily orchestrated by court appointee

definitions.text: disorder happily orchestrated by court appointee

indicators.note: letters set free from their order may fall into any new arrangement

explanation.surface: A lemur escapes into chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set free' rearranges LEMUR IS. The court appointee is the medieval Lord of Misrule, who presided over Christmas revels.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawless revelry, the merry disorder presided over by the Lord chosen to lead Christmas festivities.

clue.text: Some sentences which parse nicely can be pretty lethal

definitions.note: the definition describes a substance, a thing that can kill

indicators.note: some says only part of the following words is taken, a run of their letters

explanation.surface: Well-constructed sentences can be deadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes a run of letters from the words that follow: pARSE NICely.
explanation.definitionFit: The element is a classic poison, the killer in Arsenic and Old Lace.

clue.text: T. W. Robertson's class revealed in play

definitions.text: T. W. Robertson's class revealed in play

parts.words: T. W. Robertson's class revealed in play
parts.note: the Victorian dramatist T. W. Robertson wrote an 1867 comedy about social rank, whose one-word title means a social class

explanation.surface: A Victorian playwright exposes social rank on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigid social rank, the subject and title of Robertson's comedy about marriage across classes.

clue.text: His dramatic output was absurd

parts.note: absurd reads as ridiculous, but it means belonging to the Theatre of the Absurd

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on a playwright's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absurd' seems an insult, but Eugène Ionesco was a leading figure of the Theatre of the Absurd.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanian-French writer of The Bald Soprano was a founding Absurdist playwright.

clue.text: "King Fog masses his molecules of carbon in squadrons in the city, while he scatters them — ly in the suburbs" (Israel Zangwill)

definitions.text: "King Fog masses his molecules of carbon in squadrons in the city, while he scatters them — ly in the suburbs" (Israel Zangwill)

parts.words: "King Fog masses his molecules of carbon in squadrons in the city, while he scatters them — ly in the suburbs" (Israel Zangwill)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing adverb stem contrasts with massed, meaning thin or sparse

explanation.walkthrough: A literary fill-in from Israel Zangwill: the fog is dense in the city but thinly scattered in the suburbs, so the gap takes the word meaning slight, adding -ly.
explanation.definitionFit: Thinly or sparsely, the opposite of massed together in squadrons.

clue.text: A mold Bennett's monument gains time in law

indicators.note: gains says the first piece takes the second inside it

parts.note: The Statue was a 1908 play by Arnold Bennett (printed here as 'A mold') and Eden Phillpotts, and a statue is a monument

explanation.surface: The novelist's memorial gets extra time in legal proceedings.
explanation.walkthrough: The print reads 'A mold', a scanning slip for the novelist Arnold Bennett, co-author of the play The Statue.
explanation.definitionFit: An act passed by a legislature is a written law.

clue.text: Her husband was First Lord, though she was subject to 1 Across

definitions.text: Her husband was First Lord, though she was subject to 1 Across

parts.words: Her husband was First Lord, though she was subject to 1 Across
parts.note: Admiral Richard Howe was First Lord of the Admiralty, and his wife Mary sat for the painter at 1 Across; subject reads as obeying but means sitter for a portrait

explanation.surface: A noblewoman married to the Admiralty's chief, yet ruled by someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subject to' suggests obedience, but she was the subject of Gainsborough's portrait 'Mary, Countess Howe', now at Kenwood House in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary, wife of Earl Howe, the admiral, sat for Gainsborough's famous full-length portrait.
